sections.text: This checkpoint practices the whole unit. You will return a closure that owns a variable and changes it (Closures, Capturing and move), accept a closure that changes a variable (Capturing and move), write an iterator of your own (The Iterator trait) and then use adapters and consumers on it (Iterator adapters, Consuming iterators). You do not write main. It calls your code and prints the results.

The starter compiles, but three pieces are marked todo!(), a placeholder that panics with "not yet implemented" when it runs. The compiler shows warnings about unused variables until you are done. That is expected. The Collatz rule works like this: from a number n, the next number is n / 2 if n is even, and 3 * n + 1 if n is odd. The sequence ends after it reaches 1, and the 1 is included. For example, 6 gives 6, 3, 10, 5, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1.

make_counter: first make a variable for the running total, with let mut total = 0;. Then return a closure with move. Inside it, add step to total and give total back as the last expression. Every call of make_counter makes its own total, so two counters do not share it. sum_where: values.iter() hands out &i32, and filter hands your closure a reference to that item, so the closure sees a &&i32. Write keep(**n) to call keep with a plain i32, and end the pipeline with .sum().

Collatz::next: if done is true, return None right away. Otherwise save self.current in a variable, work out the following number (and set done when the value is 1), and return Some of the saved value. Order matters: you must return the value you saved, not the new one.

Signatures to match: make_counter(step: i32) -> impl FnMut() -> i32, sum_where(values: &[i32], mut keep: impl FnMut(i32) -> bool) -> i32, and Iterator::next for Collatz with type Item = u64. keep is FnMut, so main can pass a closure that counts its own calls. Edge cases in main: an empty slice, and a start value of 1.

exercise.prompt:
Finish the program. Three pieces are marked todo!().

(1) fn make_counter(step: i32) -> impl FnMut() -> i32 returns a closure with its own running total, which starts at 0. Each call of the closure adds step to the total and returns the new total. Two counters made by two calls of make_counter do not share a total.

(2) fn sum_where(values: &[i32], mut keep: impl FnMut(i32) -> bool) -> i32 returns the sum of the values for which keep returns true. Use an iterator pipeline, and call keep exactly once per value. The sum of no values is 0.

(3) Write fn next(&mut self) -> Option<u64> in impl Iterator for Collatz. The first item is the start value. After each item, the next one is item / 2 if it is even, and item * 3 + 1 if it is odd. After the item 1 has been given out, next returns None. The start value is always at least 1.

In this exercise you may assume that no calculation overflows.

Do not change main. When the functions work, main prints:

3 6 9
10 12
32
even total 10, checked 6
0
[6, 3, 10, 5, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1]
[1]
length from 27: 112
peak from 27: Some(9232)
[800, 400, 200, 100]

tests.label: A counter adds its step to a running total
Two counters do not share a total
sum_where adds up the values that keep accepts
keep is called exactly once per value
Collatz::new(6) gives the whole sequence down to 1
tests.code:
let steps: Vec<u64> = Collatz::new(6).collect();
check_eq!(steps, vec![6, 3, 10, 5, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1]);

tests.label: Another step value
A negative step counts down
A zero step stays at 0
Two counters with the same step
Call count with other values
Starting from 1 gives only 1
tests.code:
let steps: Vec<u64> = Collatz::new(1).collect();
check_eq!(steps, vec![1]);

tests.label: The first item is the start value
A power of two only halves
tests.code:
let steps: Vec<u64> = Collatz::new(16).collect();
check_eq!(steps, vec![16, 8, 4, 2, 1]);

tests.label: None after 1, and it stays None
Length and peak of a long sequence

hints: make_counter needs a total that lives inside the closure, so use move. sum_where uses iter, filter and sum. Collatz::next must give back the current number, not the next one, so save it before you change it.

In sum_where, filter gives your closure a reference to a reference, so call keep(**n) and end with .sum(). In next, write let value = self.current; before you change self.current, and give back Some(value).
In next, start with if self.done { return None; }. After you save value, set self.done = true when value is 1. Otherwise set self.current to value / 2 if even, or value * 3 + 1 if odd.

quiz.question: Why must the closure that make_counter returns be written with move?
options: move makes the closure run faster
move lets the closure be called more than once
Without move the closure only borrows step and total, which are gone when make_counter returns
quiz.explanation: Without move, the closure only borrows step and total, which belong to make_counter and are gone when it returns, so the compiler refuses. move gives the closure its own copies, so it can outlive the function. It has nothing to do with speed.

quiz.question: What does let it = Collatz::new(6).map(|n| n * 100); do if it is never used afterwards?
options: It runs the closure for every item right away
Nothing: map is lazy, so no item is produced and the closure never runs
It panics when the program ends
quiz.explanation: Iterator adapters like map are lazy: they only describe the work. With nothing consuming the iterator, no item is produced and the closure never runs. Rust only warns about it, and nothing panics.

quiz.question: Why does sum_where ask for mut keep: impl FnMut(i32) -> bool instead of impl Fn?
options: So the caller may pass a closure that changes a variable it captured, such as a counter
Because an Fn closure cannot return a bool
Because FnMut closures are always faster to call
quiz.explanation: FnMut allows a closure that changes what it captured, such as a counter, and sum_where can still call it many times. With impl Fn, a closure that mutates its captures would be rejected. A closure that returns bool can be Fn too, and FnMut isn't faster.
